description:
Nolan Bushnell gave engineer Allan Alcorn the job as a secret warm-up exercise, telling him it was for a General Electric contract. Alcorn had never worked on a video game before.

The paddles could not reach the top of the screen because of a defect in the circuit. Alcorn left it in on purpose. He reasoned that two skilled players could otherwise rally forever.

the bar where the prototype was tested, built around a $75 Hitachi television

A few days in, the bar's manager called Alcorn out to fix a fault. Nothing was broken: the coin mechanism was overflowing with quarters. People were coming to the bar solely to play it.

the revenue Pong consistently earned compared with other coin-operated machines.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pong: confirms Nolan Bushnell gave Allan Alcorn Pong as a secret warm-up exercise, telling him it was for a General Electric contract; that Alcorn had no prior video game experience; that a circuit defect left the paddles unable to reach the top of the screen and Alcorn kept it to limit play time; that the prototype used a $75 Hitachi black-and-white television; that it was installed at Andy Capp's Tavern in August 1972, and a few days after a fault was reported the cause proved to be the coin mechanism overflowing with quarters; that patrons came to the bar solely to play it; and that Pong consistently earned four times the revenue of other coin-operated machines.
